vocab.definition: An act that helps a person.
Treat a person and their choice with care.
Trying to make a person give in.
A limit a person wants others to respect.
Support with a task or worry.
An option a person can pick.

cases.text: A teen asks to use a pencil. The peer says no. The teen leaves it alone.
cases.next_step: The teen accepts no and can find another pencil.

cases.text: A peer laughs at a young person’s wrong answer.
cases.next_step: The young person can ask an adult for help. The peer should stop laughing at them.

cases.text: A young person says no to a game. A peer keeps asking them to join.
cases.next_step: The young person can give space or seek adult help. They do not have to join.

cases.text: A peer waits while a young person uses an aid to give a reply.
cases.next_step: Allow time and listen to the reply without speaking for the person.

cases.text: A peer says a young person must give up a snack or cannot join the group.
cases.next_step: The young person can seek adult help. Joining should not depend on giving up the snack.

cases.text: A peer says a young person’s work is rubbish.
cases.next_step: The peer should stop. The young person can seek adult support without arguing back.

asset.description: Two fictional unnamed young people sit apart at a table. An open palm supports the written refusal story. The story supplies the facts; facial expressions are not evidence of permission.

Recognise caring, unkind or pressuring behaviour and choose a helpful next step.
Owner-approved standalone RSHE outline, 26 October 2026. The approved outline is the weekly source; no separate weekly workbook row is asserted.
A teen says no. A peer still asks them to join a game. The teen does not want to join. The peer will not stop. Is this fair? Who could help?
Sort three short story cards. Choose a next step for the young person. Give a reason from the story.
RSHE-BUILD-A2-W05-E1: Behaviour choices plus one boundary or help response and a reason, with support recorded.

Print both evidence pages and all three support pages. Keep the picture whole. Cut the six story cards and the action choices. Retain the response mat. Prepare a separate adult model. Teach the symbol and word together: + care, ! harm, ? ask for help. A symbol is a cue, not a test. Use three cards covering care, unkindness and pressure before the response task.
Year A. Autumn 2 Week 5: 30 November–4 December 2026. One 40-minute RSHE lesson. No day or clock slot is inferred. This lesson is formative. Week 7 is the assessing lesson.
This helps me recognise respectful teamwork and seek support when behaviour is wrong.
Open the title before the timed sequence.
Read the fictional young person’s story.
Read the objective and success checks.
Individual task with the chosen route.
Record actual work, response and support.
Individual exit response and next step.

B offers help without requiring the young person to give in. A refusal does not need repeated defence. Saying stop is an option if safe, not a condition for getting help. The young person is not responsible for changing the peer’s behaviour. Reteach by comparing A, where no is respected, with C, where the pressure continues.

Supported: sort A, B and C with two choices at a time and adult reading. Choose a help or boundary action for C and select a matching reason. Record each prompt. Independent: sort the six cards, choose a response for C or E, and explain the choice using a detail from the story. Aspire: retain the sort and response, explain why repeated asking after no is pressure, and compare a helpful response in a new story.

Use four minutes to sort A, B and C into caring, unkind or pressuring behaviour. Use five minutes to choose a boundary or help action for C and give a story-based reason. Use three minutes to try D, E or F and check whether asking once differs from pressure after no. A learner may point or use an aid while an adult reads and records.
Read aloud, point, scribe exact words or use the usual communication aid. Record support without treating speech speed or handwriting as the target.

All teaching prompts concern fictional young people. Never ask about a learner’s own body, family or experiences. No touching, personal role-play or real-life comparisons are required. An adult may narrate both fictional parts while the learner chooses or explains a response. Respect a pass, pause or use of an aid without asking why. If a real concern arises, listen calmly and follow the setting’s safeguarding procedure promptly. Do not promise secrecy or use a disclosure as lesson evidence. Safety is the adult’s responsibility; a child is never to blame for another person’s harmful act.

Keep the actual sorting choices for at least three cards covering caring, unkind and pressuring behaviour. Keep one boundary or help response with a reason linked to C or E. Record the response mode, prompts and changes. A category label alone does not show the next step. A copied model is not individual evidence.

Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // self-edit · ? read back · R responded · E evidence in the evidence record. R requires Voice, Audience, a specific NS+ prompt and the learner response in their own colour. E is recorded only when actual work is banked. Record prompts and unfinished work. Blank sheets and adult models are not completed learner evidence.

Space: calm seating and clear resources. Voice: an optional response about the fictional case. Audience: an adult listens or reads and responds. Influence: record any change to the task support or next teaching step. A pass is respected and does not require an explanation.

S: consider dignity and choice. M: distinguish caring actions from harm and pressure. So: consider respectful teamwork and help. IL: respect a choice to pass or use an aid. MR: respect another person’s refusal and support needs. No other thread is claimed.
A fictional help request and adult reply may be offered to the Communication portfolio. Keep the learner’s actual words, choice or aid response. Staff confirm any mapping.

A, B and C provide the core contrast. D reinforces accessible caring behaviour. E adds a threat of exclusion; F is an unkind comment. Accept more than one justified category for a harmful act, especially where pressure is also unkind. Judge the explanation and next step, not rigid labels. Do not describe a whole person as bad.

A gift, friendly face or apology does not cancel pressure. A single respectful request can be fine; asking repeatedly to wear someone down is pressure. A young person can seek help without first confronting the person. The young person is not to blame if they freeze, agree under pressure or cannot speak.
